skill.name: code-style-enforcer
skill.description: Reviews code for project-specific style consistency, naming, organization, formatting, and conventions beyond standard linters.
skill.summary: Reviews code style and recommends consistent project conventions.
skill.author: CrazyDubya

security_audit.summary: Static detections are false positives caused by markdown code fences, inline code, JavaScript template strings, relative import examples, and style guide prose. content.value_statement: Teams lose time when code follows different local habits. This skill reviews files against project conventions and recommends consistent style improvements.
actual_capabilities: Detects common style configuration files for JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Go, and Java.
Reviews naming, file organization, comments, imports, error handling, and type usage patterns.
Compares code against existing project conventions and explicit contribution guides.
Provides prioritized recommendations for consistency, readability, and maintainability issues.
Suggests formatter and linter tools such as Prettier, Black, gofmt, RuboCop, and ESLint.
Can propose an EditorConfig baseline when a project lacks shared editor settings.
limitations: It does not run linters, formatters, tests, or shell commands by itself.
It cannot guarantee semantic correctness after style edits without project tests.
It depends on available project files and may need user guidance when conventions conflict.
It focuses on style and readability, not security review or performance tuning.

use_cases.title: Review a Pull Request
use_cases.description: Find naming, formatting, and organization issues before a reviewer spends time on style comments.

use_cases.title: Standardize a Legacy Module
use_cases.description: Compare older files with current project conventions and suggest small, focused cleanup steps.

use_cases.title: Create Team Style Guidance
use_cases.description: Turn repeated style choices into practical rules for contributors and onboarding documents.

prompt_templates.title: Basic Style Review
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of one file or small change.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use code-style-enforcer to review this file for naming, formatting, organization, and comment consistency. Return prioritized suggestions.

prompt_templates.title: Match Existing Conventions
prompt_templates.scenario: Apply conventions already used in the repository.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use code-style-enforcer to inspect nearby files and style configs, then recommend changes that make this code match the project.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a Pull Request
prompt_templates.scenario: Review a change before human review.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use code-style-enforcer to review this branch for style-only issues. Separate required consistency fixes from optional readability improvements.

prompt_templates.title: Define a Style Plan
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced team workflow for a mixed or legacy codebase.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use code-style-enforcer to identify conflicting conventions across this project and propose a phased plan for consistent style enforcement.

output_examples.input: A developer asks for a style review of a user service file.
output: High priority: align method order with nearby service files.
Medium priority: rename vague temporary variables to domain terms.
Low priority: make comment format match the project docstring style.

output_examples.input: A team wants consistent formatting across a TypeScript module.
output: The module mixes default and named exports without a clear pattern.
Imports should follow external, internal, then relative grouping.
The existing Prettier settings should be treated as the source of truth.

output_examples.input: A maintainer asks how to document project style rules.
output: Create a short style guide with naming, file layout, import order, and comment rules.
Reference the formatter and linter configuration files from the guide.
Add examples for the most common review comments.

best_practices: Start with existing configuration files before proposing new conventions.
Prioritize changes that improve consistency across similar files.
Keep style edits separate from behavior changes when possible.
anti_patterns: Do not rewrite working code only to satisfy personal style preferences.
Do not mix formatting changes with unrelated feature work.
Do not override explicit project conventions without a clear reason.

faq.question: Does this skill replace linters or formatters?
faq.answer: No. It complements tools like ESLint, Prettier, Black, and gofmt by reviewing conventions they may miss.

faq.question: Can it edit files directly?
faq.answer: Yes, when the environment allows Edit. Review diffs because style changes can still affect readability and maintenance.

faq.question: Which languages does it cover?
faq.answer: It includes guidance for JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Go, Java, and general style patterns.

faq.question: How does it choose a style rule?
faq.answer: It first checks project configuration and documentation, then samples nearby code for consistent patterns.

faq.question: Can it create a style guide?
faq.answer: Yes. It can help draft practical rules for naming, imports, file organization, comments, and tooling.

faq.question: Is it useful for pull requests?
faq.answer: Yes. It can separate style issues from functional review so reviewers can focus on behavior.
